newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian PM won't block pardon for exiled prince.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian PM won't block pardon for exiled prince.

text.p: Cambodian co-Premier Hun Sen said on Saturday he would never seek amnesty for exiled Prince Norodom Sirivudh but he would not block a royal pardon for the prince.

"His majesty (King Norodom Sihanouk) can grant amnesty according to his royal privilege. It is not necessary to have any request from me, and I will not request this until the day I die. This is my steadfast position," Hun Sen told Reuters.
Hun Sen's comments came one year to the day that Sirivudh, who is the half brother of the king, was exiled to France for an alleged plot to assassinate Hun Sen.
After his exile, which was brokered by the king, the prince was sentenced in absentia to 10 years in jail in a trial international observers branded a travesty.
Sirivudh has since vowed to return to Cambodia, raising tensions between the co-premiers and grabbing the attention of Cambodia's neighbouring nations.
Analysts say the fate of Sirivudh is a severe test to Cambodia's fragile coalition government.
They point to comments from Hun Sen, who last week said he would call out troops and tanks to prevent Sirivudh from returning without amnesty.
But Hun Sen later softened his stance, saying he would welcome Sirivudh with flowers at the airport -- if he were pardoned.
Co-Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh, on the other hand, wrote a personal letter to the king on Thursday requesting that Sirivudh receive a royal pardon.
King Sihanouk has remained neutral, announcing he would not pardon Sirivudh unless both prime ministers expressed their support for amnesty.
But Hun Sen told Reuters that he would not ask the king for the pardon, leaving the onus on Sihanouk.

"For more than three years, the king has granted amnesty and commuted the sentences of prisoners without the request of either prime minister," he said, adding: "I want this case to be treated normally....I won't give instructions to the king."
Hun Sen said requests should come only through the Ministries of Justice or Interior and that interference by the prime ministers set a bad precedent.
He did note, however, one exception -- when he requested amnesty for Khmer Rouge dissident Ieng Sary, which he called a special case.
Ieng Sary was granted a royal pardon in September for his role as foreign minister in the 1975-1979 "killing fields" Khmer Rouge rule.
Ranariddh has noted that as Sirivudh "didn't kill anyone," he should be granted a pardon just like Ieng Sary.
Regardless of the amnesty question, however, Sirivudh said he remained determined to return to Cambodia.
In an interview with the French weekly Le Point, he said he would be willing to be imprisoned because he could at least get free meals.
